focus: The real trap is 'allergisch gegen' – German says allergic AGAINST, not 'to'; gegen+accusative is at most a side note
The whole phrase 'Trotz des schlechten Wetters' fills slot 1, so the verb comes straight after: gehen wir, not wir gehen – spell out the consequence, skip the bare 'V2 rule' label
With no article the adjective carries the case ending itself: 'kalten Kaffee' shows the masculine accusative -en – quote the card, plain words instead of '(masc. acc)' notation
'jeden Morgen' is accusative because bare time expressions take accusative – that's why jeder becomes jeden; the current der→den/ein→einen tip never touches the card
No article means the adjective shows gender/case itself: 'Frisches Brot' takes the -es that 'das' would otherwise carry – plain words, no '(neut. nom)' notation
'fertig' alone means both 'finished' and 'wiped out' – 'fix und fertig' intensifies it; give that logic instead of re-stating the English translation
'den' is accusative because of its role INSIDE its own clause (meine Mutter backt den Kuchen) – keep that insight, cut the '(acc. masc./dat. pl.)' notation clutter
'Heft' here means hilt/handle, not notebook – a two-meanings landmine; lead with that, not a re-gloss the English field already gives
Give the literal image: 'zwei linke Hände' = two left hands, German's version of 'all thumbs' – the current tip only repeats the meaning
'helfen' takes a dative object – in German you help TO someone: er half seiner Nachbarin; cut the '= dative fem.' notation, add the English-contrast hook
Without an article the adjective takes the ending itself: 'Heißer Tee' – say it in plain words, no 'strong nom. masc.' jargon
Separable verbs split in commands – 'zuhören' becomes 'hör ... zu' with the prefix stranded at the end; give the intuition, not just the 'Separable:' label
Give the literal image: 'ein Brett vor dem Kopf' = a board in front of your head, so you can't see what's right there – don't just repeat 'mental block'
'schon' here is a reassuring particle ('you'll manage alright'), NOT 'already' – name the two-meanings landmine; the current 4-word tip has no anchor or example
'noch nicht' = not yet, literally 'still not' – anchor on that phrase from the card; drop the generic nicht-placement rulebook that doesn't fit this sentence
